sections.title: 3. Active Evaluation
sections.text: 3. Active Evaluation Active evaluation aims to minimize a metric of ranking efficiency. This section discusses several quality metrics for online ranking algorithms, and proposes Average Generalized Ranking Error (AGRE, definition 3.3 ) as the objective that measures efficiency. At first the designer must choose an experimental context : a data generator and arguments for its parameters. The experimental context is the main component that ultimately determines the shape of the data. In this paper, we propose two models for synthetic data generation (see Section 3.2 ) and incremental access to existing data sets. A task, which may be stochastic, generates scores [LaTeX: s(v,a)\sim S_{v,a}] s ⁡ ( v , a ) ∼ S v , a s(v,a)\sim S_{v,a} , where [LaTeX: S_{v,a}] S v , a S_{v,a} is a random variable that depends on the task and the agent. Data takes the form of pairwise evaluations [LaTeX: (s(v,a_{i}),s(v,a_{j}))] ( s ⁡ ( v , a i ) , s ⁡ ( v , a j ) ) (s(v,a_{i}),s(v,a_{j})) between agents [LaTeX: a_{i},a_{j}\in A] a i , a j ∈ A a_{i},a_{j}\in A on a task [LaTeX: v\in V] v ∈ V v\in V . The main experiment loop is summarized in Algorithm 1 . There are [LaTeX: T] T T iterations. In each round [LaTeX: t\in\{1,\cdots,T\}] t ∈ { 1 , ⋯ , T } t\in\{1,\cdots,T\} , an algorithm chooses a task [LaTeX: v^{t}] v t v^{t} and two agents [LaTeX: a_{i}^{t},a_{j}^{t}] a i t , a j t a_{i}^{t},a_{j}^{t} and receives data point [LaTeX: s^{t}] s t s^{t} . The algorithm then uses [LaTeX: s^{t}] s t s^{t} and outputs a new ranking [LaTeX: \succ^{t}] ≻ t \succ^{t} . A metric of performance [LaTeX: f] f f is used to assess the performance of the ranking [LaTeX: \succ^{t}] ≻ t \succ^{t} ; we describe several in the next subsection. Metrics Many metrics can be used to assess the performance of an algorithm for active evaluation. Let us first assume the existence of a correct underlying ground truth ranking , [LaTeX: \succ^{*}] ≻ ∗ \succ^{*} (which is available when generating data synthetically). In this case, the simplest metric might be to track the Kendall-tau distance to the ground truth over time, [LaTeX: K_{d}(\succ^{t},\succ^{*})] K d ( ≻ t , ≻ ∗ ) K_{d}(\succ^{t},\succ^{*}) . To make the value less dependent on the number of agents, we could use normalized Kendall-tau distance, [LaTeX: K_{n}] K n K_{n} . However, it is common that the evaluator may only be interested in the top [LaTeX: k] k k agents (maybe first, second, and third, e.g. , [LaTeX: k=3] k = 3 k=3 ) or even more extremely only the top-performing agent ( [LaTeX: k=1] k = 1 k=1 ). In these cases, the error metric should only take into account the performance of agents within these top ranks. Denote by [LaTeX: \succ_{[k]}] ≻ [ k ] \succ_{[k]} the sub-ranking of [LaTeX: \succ] ≻ \succ including only the top [LaTeX: k] k k agents, and [LaTeX: A_{\succ_{[k]}}] A ≻ [ k ] A_{\succ_{[k]}} the set of agents among the top- [LaTeX: k] k k ranked agents. Now we generalize the ranking error to include both ranking error and top- [LaTeX: k] k k identification error: Definition 3.2 (Generalized Top- [LaTeX: k] k k Ranking Error). Let [LaTeX: A] A A be a set of agents and [LaTeX: \succ^{*}] ≻ ∗ \succ^{*} be a ground truth ranking of agents in [LaTeX: A] A A , and [LaTeX: k\in\{1,2,\cdots,m\}] k ∈ { 1 , 2 , ⋯ , m } k\in\{1,2,\cdots,m\} . The generalized top- [LaTeX: k] k k ranking error is a combination of an error for identifying the set of top- [LaTeX: k] k k agents and determining their correct rank [LaTeX: \textsc{GRE}(A,\succ,\succ^{*},k)=] GRE ( A , ≻ , ≻ ∗ , k ) = \textsc{GRE}(A,\succ,\succ^{*},k)= [LaTeX: \alpha(k)\cdot\textsc{IDE}(A,\succ,\succ^{*},k)+(1-\alpha(k))\cdot K_{n}(\succ_{k^{*}},\succ^{*}),] α ( k ) ⋅ IDE ( A , ≻ , ≻ ∗ , k ) + ( 1 − α ( k ) ) ⋅ K n ( ≻ k ∗ , ≻ ∗ ) , \alpha(k)\cdot\textsc{IDE}(A,\succ,\succ^{*},k)+(1-\alpha(k))\cdot K_{n}(\succ_{k^{*}},\succ^{*}), where [LaTeX: \alpha(k)=\frac{m-k}{m-1}\in[0,1]] α ⁡ ( k ) = m − k m − 1 ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \alpha(k)=\frac{m-k}{m-1}\in[0,1] is the weight placed on the top- [LaTeX: k] k k identification error. Since [LaTeX: \alpha(k)+(1-\alpha(k))=1] α ⁡ ( k ) + ( 1 − α ⁡ ( k ) ) = 1 \alpha(k)+(1-\alpha(k))=1 , and both [LaTeX: \textsc{IDE}(A,\succ,\succ^{*},k)] IDE ( A , ≻ , ≻ ∗ , k ) \textsc{IDE}(A,\succ,\succ^{*},k) and [LaTeX: K_{n}] K n K_{n} are in [LaTeX: [0,1]] [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , it follows that [LaTeX: \textsc{GRE}(A,\succ,\succ^{*},k)\in[0,1]] GRE ( A , ≻ , ≻ ∗ , k ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \textsc{GRE}(A,\succ,\succ^{*},k)\in[0,1] . When [LaTeX: k=1] k = 1 k=1 , all of the weight is placed on identification whereas when [LaTeX: k=m] k = m k=m all of the weight is placed on Kendall-tau distance, with linear weighting between the two error sources for other values of [LaTeX: k] k k . This linear weighting naturally places weight proportionally to favor identification error when [LaTeX: k] k k is small and Kendall-tau ranking error when [LaTeX: k] k k is large. Finally, we can also think of the average ranking error similarly to regret analysis of online learning ( Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi, 2006 ; Blum and Mansour, 2007 ; Hazan, 2015 ) : Definition 3.3 (Average Generalized Top- [LaTeX: k] k k Ranking Error). Let [LaTeX: A] A A be a set of agents, [LaTeX: \succ^{*}] ≻ ∗ \succ^{*} be a ground truth ranking of agents in [LaTeX: A] A A , and [LaTeX: k\in\{1,2,\cdots,m\}] k ∈ { 1 , 2 , ⋯ , m } k\in\{1,2,\cdots,m\} . The average generalized ranking error (AGRE) of an algorithm that outputs rankings [LaTeX: \succ^{t}] ≻ t \succ^{t} on round [LaTeX: t] t t is: [LaTeX: \textsc{AGRE}(\succ^{1:T},\succ^{*},T)=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\textsc{GRE}(A,\succ^{t},\succ^{*},k)}{T}.] AGRE ( ≻ 1 : T , ≻ ∗ , T ) = ∑ t = 1 T GRE ( A , ≻ t , ≻ ∗ , k ) T . \textsc{AGRE}(\succ^{1:T},\succ^{*},T)=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\textsc{GRE}(A,\succ^{t},\succ^{*},k)}{T}. At any horizon [LaTeX: T] T T , the AGRE provides a metric of how efficiently the ranking algorithm identifies good rankings, as it cumulates all errors at horizons [LaTeX: t<T] t < T t<T . 3.2. Models for Synthetic Data We now describe models for synthetic data generation. A key feature of using synthetic data is that the ground truth is known, hence the metrics described in Section 3.1 can be used directly. Figure 1. Mallows The Mallows model is a common way to model a number of noisy rankings from a central ranking, [LaTeX: \succ^{*}] ≻ ∗ \succ^{*} over [LaTeX: m] m m alternatives ( Mallows, 1957 ; Brandt et al., 2016 ) . Given a dispersion parameter [LaTeX: \phi\in[0,1]] ϕ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \phi\in[0,1] , when [LaTeX: \phi=0] ϕ = 0 \phi=0 only the central ranking is sampled; when [LaTeX: \phi=1] ϕ = 1 \phi=1 all rankings are equally likely. The probability of sampling a ranking [LaTeX: \succ] ≻ \succ is (4) [LaTeX: \frac{1}{Z(\phi,m)}\phi^{K_{d}(\succ^{*},\succ)},] 1 Z ⁡ ( ϕ , m ) ϕ K d ( ≻ ∗ , ≻ ) , \frac{1}{Z(\phi,m)}\phi^{K_{d}(\succ^{*},\succ)}, where [LaTeX: Z(\phi,m)] Z ⁡ ( ϕ , m ) Z(\phi,m) is a normalization constant. We then use Equation 4 to generate task rankings over models, [LaTeX: \succ^{*}_{v}] ≻ ∗ v \succ^{*}_{v} , where each task ranks models. Intuitively, if [LaTeX: \phi] ϕ \phi is close to 0, then we are more likely to draw task rankings which are close to [LaTeX: \succ^{*}] ≻ ∗ \succ^{*} as measured by Kendall-tau distance. As [LaTeX: \phi] ϕ \phi approaches 1, we are more likely to draw a more diverse set of task rankings since the effect of the Kendall-tau distance on the probability of any ranking being generated is smaller. For each task ranking [LaTeX: \succ^{*}_{v}] ≻ ∗ v \succ^{*}_{v} , [LaTeX: m] m m distributions of scores, [LaTeX: S_{v,a}] S v , a S_{v,a} for [LaTeX: a\in A] a ∈ A a\in A mentioned in Section 3 , are generated by sampling uniform random numbers in a bounded score internal and assigning the values as the means of [LaTeX: S_{v,a}] S v , a S_{v,a} ( [LaTeX: \mu_{v,a}] μ v , a \mu_{v,a} ), such that they are sorted according to [LaTeX: \succ^{*}_{v}] ≻ ∗ v \succ^{*}_{v} . Each [LaTeX: S_{v,a}] S v , a S_{v,a} is then normally-distributed according to [LaTeX: \mathcal{N}(\mu_{s,a},\sigma)] 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ s , a , σ ) \mathcal{N}(\mu_{s,a},\sigma) . A summary of the process is depicted in Figure 1 . 3.2.2. Plackett-Luce We also try an alternative synthetic data model: Plackett-Luce. sections.title: 4. Algorithms for Active Evaluation
sections.text: 4. Algorithms for Active Evaluation We now describe several algorithms which we will compare experimentally in the following section (summarized in Table 1 ). Algorithms for active evaluation are naturally decompose into three steps (with line references to Algorithm 1 ): (1) the task selection chooses a task [LaTeX: v^{t}\in V] v t ∈ V v^{t}\in V (line 1 ), (2) the agent selection chooses two agents [LaTeX: (a^{t}_{i},a^{t}_{j})] ( a i t , a j t ) (a^{t}_{i},a^{t}_{j}) (line 1 ), and (3) the process that updates tracked information based on the score sample [LaTeX: s^{t}] s t s^{t} (line 1 ). 4.1. A summary of algorithms for active evaluation. For methods based on zero-sum games, the Task Strategy and Agent Strategy are sampling distributions in the underlying game, \ie with uniform exploration mixed in: e.g. , [LaTeX: \sigma^{\prime}(a)=\frac{\epsilon}{|A|}+(1-\epsilon)\sigma] σ ′ ​ ( a ) = ϵ | A | + ( 1 − ϵ ) ​ σ \sigma^{\prime}(a)=\frac{\epsilon}{|A|}+(1-\epsilon)\sigma . The most basic procedure for steps (1) and (2) is UniformRandom which samples [LaTeX: v\sim\textsc{Uniform}(V)] v ∼ Uniform ​ ( V ) v\sim\textsc{Uniform}(V) uniformly at random and [LaTeX: (a_{i},a_{j})\sim\textsc{Uniform}(A)] ( a i , a j ) ∼ Uniform ​ ( A ) (a_{i},a_{j})\sim\textsc{Uniform}(A) without replacement. The simplest update rule tracks the cumulative average score [LaTeX: \bar{S}_{a}] S ¯ a \bar{S}_{a} aggregated across all tasks and outputs a ranking [LaTeX: \succ^{t}] ≻ t \succ^{t} by sorting [LaTeX: \bar{S}_{a}] S ¯ a \bar{S}_{a} for [LaTeX: a\in A] a ∈ A a\in A . Denote this simplest baseline algorithm UniformAveraging . A second baseline, BatchElo is based on the Elo rating system: it also samples tasks and agents uniformly randomly, and maintains a historical record of win/loss outcomes where [LaTeX: s(v^{t},a^{t}_{i})>s(v^{t},a^{t}_{j})] s ⁡ ( v t , a i t ) > s ⁡ ( v t , a j t ) s(v^{t},a^{t}_{i})>s(v^{t},a^{t}_{j}) counts as a win for [LaTeX: a_{i}] a i a_{i} and loss for [LaTeX: a_{j}] a j a_{j} . Then an efficient batch implementation of Elo ( Hunter, 2004 ) computes the best fit for ratings [LaTeX: \boldsymbol{\theta}] 𝜽 \boldsymbol{\theta} and [LaTeX: \succ^{t}] ≻ t \succ^{t} is obtained by sorting the ratings in descending order. We also use OnlineElo , the standard update typically used on competitive gaming platforms from single-game outcomes. 4.1.1. Stochastic Bandit-based Approaches We suggest bandit-based approaches based on Upper Confidence Bounds (UCB) algorithm ( Auer et al., 2002 ) as often used in Monte Carlo tree search ( Kocsis and Szepesvári, 2006 ) . BasicUCB is a single multi-armed bandit with one arm assigned to each agent (scores aggregated across tasks. Each agent [LaTeX: a\in A] a ∈ A a\in A is assigned a UCB score: [LaTeX: \textsc{UCBScore}(a,T)=\bar{s}_{a}+C\sqrt{\log(2T)/T_{a}},] UCBScore ​ ( a , T ) = s ¯ a + C ​ log ⁡ ( 2 ​ T ) / T a , \textsc{UCBScore}(a,T)=\bar{s}_{a}+C\sqrt{\log(2T)/T_{a}}, where [LaTeX: \bar{s}_{a}] s ¯ a \bar{s}_{a} is the average score of agent [LaTeX: a] a a , [LaTeX: C] C C is a constant set to [LaTeX: \sqrt{2}\Delta_{S}] 2 ​ Δ S \sqrt{2}\Delta_{S} , [LaTeX: 2T] 2 ​ T 2T is the total number of updates and, [LaTeX: T_{a}] T a T_{a} is the number of updates to agent [LaTeX: a] a a . Tasks are selected uniformly at random. The final ranking is a sorting of visit counts per arm. 4.1.2. Dueling Bandit Approaches When using a dueling bandit ( Yue et al., 2012 ) approach feedback comes in the form of a preference between the two arms pulled. Dueling bandits have been used for ranking, for example Copeland dueling bandits ( Zoghi et al., 2015 ) . We use a recent dueling bandit based on Kemeny ranking called KemenyEl ( George and Dimitrakakis, 2024 , Algorithm 1) . Like UCB, KemenyEl uses statistics to estimate the noise between pairwise preferences, factoring it into its decision rule. Unlike UCB, the Kemeny rule is used for ranking. We adapt KemenyEl to the online evaluation setting in the following way. The approximation accuracy of KemenyEl holds with probability [LaTeX: 1-\delta] 1 − δ 1-\delta , where [LaTeX: \delta] δ \delta is chosen by the user and determines the number of samples per pairwise matchup. In the online setting, we first choose an initial [LaTeX: \delta_{0}=0.1] δ 0 = 0.1 \delta_{0}=0.1 ; once the number of samples per matchup is reached ( \ie one matchup per round of Alg. 1 ), a new epoch is started ( [LaTeX: k\leftarrow k+1] k ← k + 1 k\leftarrow k+1 ) and we set [LaTeX: \delta_{k}=\frac{\delta_{k-1}}{2}] δ k = δ k − 1 2 \delta_{k}=\frac{\delta_{k-1}}{2} . Similarly, we set the acceptable Kendall-tau distance error, [LaTeX: \rho_{0}] ρ 0 \rho_{0} , to be half of the total Kendall-tau distance and then halve it every epoch. 4.2. Growing Batch and Online Algorithms Any algorithm that is normally run offline ( \ie on an evaluation data set) can be run online by simply collecting evaluation data over time and running the algorithm on the data set on iteration [LaTeX: t] t t . We call this the growing-batch version of an offline algorithm. Voting-as-Evaluation methods interpret evaluations as data sets similarly to how Elo does: for example, given two score samples for task [LaTeX: v] v v if, [LaTeX: s(v^{t},a^{t}_{i})>s(v^{t},a^{t}_{j})] s ⁡ ( v t , a i t ) > s ⁡ ( v t , a j t ) s(v^{t},a^{t}_{i})>s(v^{t},a^{t}_{j}) , this counts as a vote [LaTeX: a_{i}\succ a_{j}] a i ≻ a j a_{i}\succ a_{j} . Given the pairwise preference collection, we examine several Condorcet methods: BatchCopeland , BatchRankedPairs , and BatchMaximalLotteries corresponding to growing-batch versions of the Copeland, Ranked Pairs, and Maximal Lotteries voting schemes ( Copeland, 1951 ; Tideman, 1987 ; Fishburn, 1984 ; Lanctot et al., 2023 ) . We use an iterative variant of Maximal Lotteries ( Lanctot et al., 2023 ) which provides a ranking over agents. We also use a batch version of Soft Condorcet Optimization ( Lanctot et al., 2025 ) , which is a gradient descent algorithm run on a smooth Kendall-tau loss and its fully-online version which is analogous to Elo’s standard online update. We introduce a new fully-online version of Maximal Lotteries that we describe separately in Section 4.2.2 . A different way to apply VasE algorithms online is to use a mean model . Mean-model VasE algorithms maintain [LaTeX: nm] n ​ m nm emprical averages of each score [LaTeX: \bar{s}_{v,a}] s ¯ v , a \bar{s}_{v,a} . Estimated per-task agent rankings [LaTeX: \hat{\succ}_{v}] ≻ ^ v \hat{\succ}_{v} are obtained by sorting [LaTeX: \bar{s}_{v,a}] s ¯ v , a \bar{s}_{v,a} for [LaTeX: a\in A] a ∈ A a\in A ; then, a voting rule returns a ranking from the [LaTeX: n] n n ranked-ballot votes. ProportionalRepresentation is a mean-model adaptation of the recently-proposed Greedy Metritocracy algorithm ( Procaccia et al., 2025 , Algorithm 1) . In particular, it uses estimated task ranking [LaTeX: \hat{\succ}_{v}] ≻ ^ v \hat{\succ}_{v} as votes to determine an evaluation set : a group (subset) of tasks that are the “most representative”, recomputing this subset on each iteration based on updated estimates. Task selection is then uniformly at random from among the evaluation set, with a small probability (0.1) of choosing uniformly form the entire set of tasks to ensure exploration. The reported ranking is then obtained by running Ranked Pairs votes over the votes from estimated task rankings. All of the mean-model and growing-batch algorithm use a burn-in phase: for the first [LaTeX: nm] n ​ m nm iterations, the task and agent sampling one cycle through a uniform shuffling of the unique [LaTeX: (v,a)\in V\times A] ( v , a ) ∈ V × A (v,a)\in V\times A pairs. This burn-in phase has been shown to benefit stochastic gradient descent algorithms ( Roux et al., 2013 ) . Data is still collected and rankings reported in the same way during the burn-in period. 4.2.1. Growing Batch Nash Averaging One way to define ratings of players is to analyze the one-shot meta-game played between agents and tasks ( Balduzzi et al., 2018 ) . This matrix game is a two-player zero-sum game where the row player chooses an agent [LaTeX: a\in A] a ∈ A a\in A and the column player chooses a task [LaTeX: v\in V] v ∈ V v\in V . The utility to the row player for the joint choice [LaTeX: (a,v)] ( a , v ) (a,v) is the score [LaTeX: s_{v,a}] s v , a s_{v,a} and the utility to the column player is [LaTeX: -s_{v,a}] − s v , a -s_{v,a} . In the original paper, these utilities where averaged over many samples, so utilities took the form e.g. , [LaTeX: (\bar{s}_{v,a},-\bar{s}_{v,a})] ( s ¯ v , a , − s ¯ v , a ) (\bar{s}_{v,a},-\bar{s}_{v,a}) . The rating of agent [LaTeX: a] a a , [LaTeX: \theta_{a}] θ a \theta_{a} , is defined as the expected utility of strategy [LaTeX: a] a a versus the task player’s Nash equilibrium strategy, which can be computed efficiently (polynomial time) since the game is two-player zero-sum. A growing-batch version employs Nash averaging on the batch of data collected so far: utilities are averages, and it computes ratings as in the original Nash averaging. A ranking is then obtained by sorting the ratings. Nash averaging can be also run fully online by using adversarial bandits. We elaborate on this in the next section. 4.2.2. Online Max. Lotteries and Nash Averaging Similarly to Nash averaging, the Maximal Lotteries voting method also involves solving a two-player zero-sum “margin game” and using its solution to define the set of winners. The game is an two-player zero-sum agent-vs-agent game: the utility to the row player for strategy [LaTeX: a_{i}] a i a_{i} versus the column player’s choice [LaTeX: a_{j}] a j a_{j} is the voter margin [LaTeX: \delta(a_{i},a_{j})=N(a_{i},a_{j})-N(a_{j},a_{i})] δ ⁡ ( a i , a j ) = N ⁡ ( a i , a j ) − N ⁡ ( a j , a i ) \delta(a_{i},a_{j})=N(a_{i},a_{j})-N(a_{j},a_{i}) , where [LaTeX: N(a_{i},a_{j})] N ⁡ ( a i , a j ) N(a_{i},a_{j}) is the number of votes where [LaTeX: a_{i}\succ a_{j}] a i ≻ a j a_{i}\succ a_{j} . As above, the growing-batch version of Maximal Lotteries derives this game from the growing data set; like Nash averaging, it can also be run fully online. We defer the details of solving two-player zero-sum games using adversarial bandits to Appendix A . We base our implementations on regret-matching ( Hart and Mas-Colell, 2001 ) . In Nash averaging, when agent [LaTeX: i] i i is sampled against task [LaTeX: v^{t}] v t v^{t} the utility is [LaTeX: s(v^{t},a_{i})] s ⁡ ( v t , a i ) s(v^{t},a_{i}) (obtained in Line 1 of Algorithm 1 ). The solution to the game (approximate Nash equilibrium) is extracted as a pair of distributions (stochastic strategies) [LaTeX: \sigma=(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})] σ = ( σ 1 , σ 2 ) \sigma=(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}) for players 1 and 2. In the case of Nash averaging, [LaTeX: \sigma_{1}\in\Delta(A)] σ 1 ∈ Δ ⁡ ( A ) \sigma_{1}\in\Delta(A) and [LaTeX: \sigma_{2}\in\Delta(V)] σ 2 ∈ Δ ⁡ ( V ) \sigma_{2}\in\Delta(V) . In the case of Maximal Lotteries, [LaTeX: \sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\in\Delta(A)] σ 1 , σ 2 ∈ Δ ⁡ ( A ) \sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\in\Delta(A) where [LaTeX: \Delta(A)] Δ ⁡ ( A ) \Delta(A) represents a simplex over elements in [LaTeX: A] A A . The utility for the row player choosing [LaTeX: a_{i}] a i a_{i} playing against column player choosing [LaTeX: a_{j}] a j a_{j} when task [LaTeX: v^{t}] v t v^{t} was sampled (uniformly) is: [LaTeX: \hat{u}_{i}(v^{t},a_{i},a_{j})=2\cdot\mathbb{I}[s(v^{t},a_{i})>s(v^{t},a_{j})]-1] u ^ i ( v t , a i , a j ) = 2 ⋅ 𝕀 [ s ( v t , a i ) > s ( v t , a j ) ] − 1 \hat{u}_{i}(v^{t},a_{i},a_{j})=2\cdot\mathbb{I}[s(v^{t},a_{i})>s(v^{t},a_{j})]-1 , where [LaTeX: \mathbb{I}] 𝕀 \mathbb{I} is the indicator function. In both cases (Nash averaging and Maximal Lotteries), to extract a ranking, we define the ratings as expected values against the equilibrium strategy; e.g. , for [LaTeX: a\in A] a ∈ A a\in A : [LaTeX: \textsc{Rating}(a)=\mathbb{E}_{b\sim\sigma_{2}}u_{1}(a,b)] Rating ​ ( a ) = 𝔼 b ∼ σ 2 ​ u 1 ​ ( a , b ) \textsc{Rating}(a)=\mathbb{E}_{b\sim\sigma_{2}}u_{1}(a,b) , where [LaTeX: u_{1}(a,b)] u 1 ​ ( a , b ) u_{1}(a,b) is the average utility to player 1 given choices [LaTeX: a] a a and [LaTeX: b] b b as described in the games above. The rankings are then extracted by sorting the ratings. This naturally extends Maximal Lotteries’ distribution over winner agents to a ranking among agents ( Marris et al., 2022 ) . 4.3. Summary of Known Convergence Results Since the game online Nash Averaging plays is a sample-based version of the true underlying game, the average strategy used by adversarial bandits is guaranteed to converge to an approximate equilibrium with high probability, and the error decreases as [LaTeX: \epsilon_{t}=O(1/\sqrt{t})] ϵ t = O ⁡ ( 1 / t ) \epsilon_{t}=O(1/\sqrt{t}) where [LaTeX: t] t t is the number of iterations ( Auer et al., 1998 ) , and ratings will differ from the true ratings by at most [LaTeX: \epsilon_{t}] ϵ t \epsilon_{t} . Similarly, the solution computed by Batch Maximal Lotteries is obtained by solving a two-player zero-sum margin game derived directly from a preference profile. The error of the estimated expected utility of a cell in the margin game (defined in Section 4.2.2 ) decreases as [LaTeX: O(1/\sqrt{t})] O ⁡ ( 1 / t ) O(1/\sqrt{t}) and hence the Maximal Lottery solution we derive from it will be a [LaTeX: O(1/\sqrt{t})] O ⁡ ( 1 / t ) O(1/\sqrt{t}) -approximate solution. Asymptotic guarantees on GRE requires knowing the ground truth and, possibly, also the shape of the data both of which are generally not known. When data is shaped as described in Sec 3.2.1 , the mean model variants’ estimated means converge to the true means of the underlying score distributions at a rate of [LaTeX: 1/\sqrt{n}] 1 / n 1/\sqrt{n} by the Monte Carlo square root law; consequently, the estimated task rankings will converge to the true task rankings and the overall ranking to a VasE-aggregated one from the task rankings.

Each line is a mean over the same 100 seeds with 95% confidence intervals in shaded area. Each data point is a sliding-window average of the most recent 250 values of GRE for the reported ranking [LaTeX: \succ^{t}] ≻ t \succ^{t} at iteration [LaTeX: t] t t . The top two graphs use dispersion [LaTeX: \phi=0.3] ϕ = 0.3 \phi=0.3 , with [LaTeX: k\in\{3,8\}] k ∈ { 3 , 8 } k\in\{3,8\} , where [LaTeX: k=8] k = 8 k=8 corresponds to normalized Kendall-tau distance. The bottom two use [LaTeX: \phi=0.6] ϕ = 0.6 \phi=0.6 and vary [LaTeX: k] k k similarly. We now compare the performance of each active evaluation algorithm, first on synthetic data then on real Atari agent data. 5.1. Experiments with Synthetic Data For experiments using synthetic data using models described in Section 3.2 . For score distributions, means are drawn from the interval [LaTeX: \mu_{v,a}\in[0,100]] μ v , a ∈ [ 0,100 ] \mu_{v,a}\in[0,100] and use standard deviation of [LaTeX: \sigma=20] σ = 20 \sigma=20 . 5.1.1. Experimental Condition 1: Ranking Error Reduction Rate A primary motivation of research on active evaluation is designing algorithms that use/sample data efficiently, so a main research question is how well algorithms can report a ranking that is close to the ground truth as a function of number of samples. We use a moderately sized problem with [LaTeX: m=8] m = 8 m=8 agents and [LaTeX: n=50] n = 50 n=50 tasks; each seed determines a new ground truth ranking, task rankings, and score distributions. Since the fully-online variants of algorithms are approximating the growing-batch versions, we restrict this first experiment to the growing batch algorithms with basic baselines and bandit approaches. Figure 2 shows the generalized top- [LaTeX: k] k k ranking error (GRE, definition 3.2 ) as a function if iterations of Algorithm 1 . Our first observation is that, when [LaTeX: k=3] k = 3 k=3 , it is possible to drive the error to 0 within 2000 iterations and several algorithms achieve this. Our second observation, UniformAveraging – the most basic of baselines– performs particularly well in all settings, and in three of four cases is reduces the error fastest in the first 1000 iterations, though BasicUCB has comparable performance when [LaTeX: \phi=0.6] ϕ = 0.6 \phi=0.6 . In general, UniformAveraging , BasicUCB , BatchElo , BatchSCO , and ProportionalRepresentation reduce the error most quickly at the beginning. In Nash averaging, we observe a phenomenon similar to “adversarial task selection” reported in ( Lanctot et al., 2023 ) : since it is a zero-sum game of agents versus tasks, the task player prefers to choose tasks where the agents’ utilities are minimized, resulting in an equilibrium distribution skewed towards task rankings that may be arbitrarily far from the ground truth. Hence, the ranking overfits to these adversarially-chosen tasks. When [LaTeX: \phi=0.6] ϕ = 0.6 \phi=0.6 , ProportionalRepresentation is a clear winner, deviating significantly from the other methods, which could be due to its reduced evaluation set, removal of tasks that are less representative. In Table 2 , we report on the longer-term performance in the form of average GRE at [LaTeX: t=10000] t = 10000 t=10000 for [LaTeX: \phi=0.3] ϕ = 0.3 \phi=0.3 and [LaTeX: k\in\{3,8\}] k ∈ { 3 , 8 } k\in\{3,8\} , which can be interpreted as an approximate average area-under-the-GRE-curve. We observe that BasicUCB and UniformAveraging peform best when [LaTeX: k=3] k = 3 k=3 and UniformAveraging performs best when [LaTeX: k=8] k = 8 k=8 . In both cases, BatchElo also reduces the rank error at a fast rate. Experimental Condition 2: Batch versus Online Firstly, we see that there are several methods that reach 0 error in less than 10000 iterations: BatchSCO , BatchElo , OnlineElo , ProportionalRepresentation , and all of the mean-model variants. Second, while the batch version of Maximal Lotteries reduces rank error faster than its online variant, in Nash averaging this is reversed, possibly due to the average strategy in the adversarial bandit changing more smoothly. Third, mean-model variants and ProportionalRepresentation reduce error rate faster than the batch versions of these algorithms, several reaching 0 error in less than 6000 iterations ( MeanModelMaximalLotteries and MeanModelRankedPairs ). Figure 3. Exp Condition 2: Generalized top- [LaTeX: k] k k ranking error (GRE) over iterations for several algorithms. Each data point is a sliding-window average of the most recent 250 values of GRE for the reported ranking [LaTeX: \succ^{t}] ≻ t \succ^{t} at iteration [LaTeX: t] t t . Both graphs use [LaTeX: k=3] k = 3 k=3 . Please note the log scale for both axes. 5.2. Experiments with Real Data In this section, we simulate the online sampling of evaluation data by presenting theses data sets as data generators. 5.2.1. Atari We use previos results of agents playing all 57 classic Atari games via the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) ( Bellemare et al., 2013 ) . In particular, we use the data from the “Agent57 paper” table in ( Badia et al., 2020 , Section H.4) which comprises [LaTeX: m=8] m = 8 m=8 agents and [LaTeX: n=57] n = 57 n=57 tasks (Atari games). The agents are varied among uniform random, human expert, and several deep reinforcement learning algorithms. In particular, unlike much of the previous work on deep reinforcement learning in ALE, this table reports both mean scores [LaTeX: \mu_{v,a}] μ v , a \mu_{v,a} and standard deviations [LaTeX: \sigma_{v,a}] σ v , a \sigma_{v,a} . Hence, we simulate a data generator by setting the score distributions [LaTeX: S_{v,a}=\mathcal{N}(\mu_{v,a},\sigma_{v,a})] S v , a = 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ v , a , σ v , a ) S_{v,a}=\mathcal{N}(\mu_{v,a},\sigma_{v,a}) where [LaTeX: \mathcal{N}] 𝒩 \mathcal{N} is a normal distribution, and otherwise identically to the synthetic data generators. Since the scale of rewards is different in each game, we also linearly normalize the scores per game from range [LaTeX: [\min_{a\in A}\mu_{v,a},\max_{a\in A}\mu_{v,a}]] [ min a ∈ A ⁡ μ v , a , max a ∈ A ⁡ μ v , a ] [\min_{a\in A}\mu_{v,a},\max_{a\in A}\mu_{v,a}] to within range [LaTeX: [0,100]] [ 0,100 ] [0,100] . This score normalization does not affect the task rankings, is required by Nash averaging ( Balduzzi et al., 2018 ) and averaging methods, and helps maintain a consistent interval for exploration constant in bandit methods. In the absence of a proper ground truth we compute the ranking that minimizes the average Kendall-tau distance to the data: [LaTeX: \succ^{*}=\min_{\succ^{\prime}}\frac{1}{57}\sum_{v\in V}K_{d}(\succ^{\prime},\succ_{v})] ≻ ∗ = min ≻ ′ 1 57 ∑ v ∈ V K d ( ≻ ′ , ≻ v ) \succ^{*}=\min_{\succ^{\prime}}\frac{1}{57}\sum_{v\in V}K_{d}(\succ^{\prime},\succ_{v}) ; this ranking is a maximum likelihood estimator of the ground truth under a Mallows model ( Brandt et al., 2016 , Chapter 8) . We also show in Appendix B.1 that it also recovers the ground truth ranking on synthetic data. The average generalized top- [LaTeX: k] k k ranking error is summarized in Table 3 (for full graphs of GRE over iterations, see Figure 8 in Appendix C ). In this setting, BatchSCO performed best followed by OnlineSCO and five of the top six were VasE methods. The order of the simple baselines BasicUCB and UniformAveraging is completely reversed from the synthetic data setting: they perform worst in Atari; this indicates that in some domains one may need to be careful when aggregating scores across tasks. Nash averaging also performs poorly, which could also be due to the adversarially-chosen task distribution. We do note that there are [LaTeX: \frac{15}{57}] 15 57 \frac{15}{57} tasks whose rankings different significantly from the ground truth, \ie where [LaTeX: K_{d}(\succ^{*}_{v},\succ^{*})\geq 8] K d ( ≻ v ∗ , ≻ ∗ ) ≥ 8 K_{d}(\succ^{*}_{v},\succ^{*})\geq 8 ; skewing a task distribution toward any of these high-distance tasks could significantly hinder the ability to find the ground truth ranking. We compare the task variation from the ground truth to samples from the synthetic data in Appendix B .
